newsitem.title: USA: Latvia vows to work hard on NATO, EU membership.
newsitem.headline: Latvia vows to work hard on NATO, EU membership.

text.p: Latvian President Guntis Ulmanis said on Friday Latvia would do everything possible to be included in NATO's next round of expansion after being rejected by the alliance last month.

Ulmanis also said Latvia still hoped to persuade the European Union to allow it to enter among the first group of east European countries even though it was not selected by the European Commission last month.
In an interview with Reuters during a visit to San Francisco, Ulmanis said he hoped the process of Latvian accession to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) could begin in 1999.
"Maybe that's a bold statement, but we'll do everything to have some grounds (for that)," he said through an interpreter, adding that the accession process could take another two or three years.
In Madrid last month, NATO leaders invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to begin entry talks.
They mentioned Romania and Slovenia as deserving cases when the enlargement process is renewed in 1999 and held out future hopes to the Baltic states, which include Latvia.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin has said that admitting former Soviet Baltic states into the Western alliance would endanger Russian security and Moscow would strongly oppose it.

"Of course Yeltsin has every right to express what he has said. But it's good luck that now in Europe and in the world the development processes are not going on just taking into consideration the Russian point of view only," Ulmanis said.
"In my opinion ... this process cannot be stopped," he said, refering to NATO expansion.
Ulmanis was in San Francisco for the annual meeting of the American Bar Association to receive the 1997 Central and East European Law Initiative award, presented for his support for legal reform.

The European Commission recommended this month that five east European nations, including Latvia's neighbour Estonia, should be invited to take part in talks on joining the European Union. Latvia and four other countries would have a separate status allowing them to prepare for membership at their own pace. EU leaders take a final decision in December.
Ulmanis said it would be "much more honest and much more pleasant if we were also nominated among those first countries.

"But what has happened actually will mobilise and stimulate us for doing everything more actively than before. We shall continue to work intensively with all the issues pertaining to the criteria of the EU," he said.

The road to EU membership was "not some kind of short distance running. It's more a long distance running ... There is a possibility somehow to overtake another runner and I think that Latvia will try to do that," he said.
He said Latvia still hoped to persuade the EU to allow it to enter among first group of east European countries.
Ulmanis said the recent change of prime minister in Latvia would not affect the pace of reform and could speed it up.
Guntar Krasts won the backing of leading political parties and the president this week to be prime minister, replacing Andris Shkele.
"I cannot name even one direction where something could change, maybe only the fact that the reforms will go on even faster than up to now," Ulmanis said.

Asked if legislative changes were possible to encourage Russian speakers in Latvia to naturalise as citizens, Ulmanis said Latvia's citizenship law and naturalisation regulations were very liberal compared to many European countries.

"Still, taking into consideration the fact that the naturalisation process is rather slow I would like to ask the political forces to pay greater attention to this issue and if need be to make necessary changes," he said.
